cards.title: Run a Rebrand as a Decision About What to Keep, Not Just What to Change
cards.summary: Use an explicit keep/change inventory to justify a rebrand and protect existing brand equity
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to rebrand an existing store or product line that already sells, or scoping what a redesign should touch
steps: State why you are changing anything: the source's framing is that even a healthy business updates its brand because its opinions, values, and market understanding have sharpened over time, not because growth stalled. Write down the questions driving your review, e.g. where have we been, what is our vision, how do we stand out, what is worth keeping, what must change to grow. ['Where have we been in the last five years, and what's our vision for the future?', 'How might we position our brand and products to be distinct in the marketplace?', 'What's worth keeping and what needs to change for our business to grow?']

Treat the brand as the customer's gut feeling about you, shaped by every touchpoint, rather than as logo, colors and typefaces. Checklist what each touchpoint currently communicates before redesigning any of them, so visual changes stay connected to perception.

Run the work through the Double Diamond: Discover (research and data gathering), Define (synthesize into a clear design challenge), Develop (explore directions, e.g. stylescapes), Deliver (refine and roll out). In the source's case study, this ran several weeks for strategy and roughly four months before rollout began, with rollout continuing for months after.

Explicitly audit brand equity before replacing assets. In the Mode case study, the logo was kept and only slightly refined because it worked and equity had been built around it; the emphasis went to usage detail rather than replacement. Apply the same test to your own logo, product names, and packaging: keep what carries recognition, change what blocks your goal.

Expect revamping to include catalog decisions. The source's Define phase resulted in discontinuing certain products to sharpen focus on better ones — treat assortment as part of the brand decision, not a separate merchandising task.
caveats: This is one company's documented process (Mode, 2025, several weeks of strategy work), not a benchmark for timeline or outcome.
A rebrand is not a guaranteed revenue driver; the source explicitly notes impact takes time to see.

cards.title: XY Competitive Mapping to Find Crowded Pools and Open Space
cards.summary: Plot competitors and out-of-industry brands on opposing-qualities axes to locate an ownable position
cards.use_when: Positioning a store or product line against competitors, or refreshing an existing position that feels undifferentiated
steps: Define the brand's attributes first (values and beliefs, features and benefits, voice and tone, look and feel) using focused prompts and free brainstorming; group similar ideas into word clusters and prioritize what resonates most with the team.

Describe positioning as the space the brand occupies in the hearts and minds of customers relative to competitors, then build an X/Y map with opposing brand qualities on each axis. Voice examples from the source: understated vs. outspoken, opaque company vs. transparent and human. Aesthetic examples: warm and inviting vs. stark and industrial, highly curated vs. raw and unedited, premium vs. budget or standard.
Plot both direct competitors and brands from other industries on the grid. The out-of-category brands reveal visual and tonal space that keyboard- or category-only comparison hides.

Read the map for crowded pools — the source found Mode was swimming in a crowded pool in some areas with little to set it apart, which triggered the questions of how to carve out unique space and what must change to create distinction. Use those two questions as the output of the exercise.

Translate the resulting open space into one or two concrete positioning themes, e.g. the source's 'Warm Tech' (making technology feel human and inviting) and 'creating joy in everyday experiences'. Carry these forward as filters for later visual and messaging decisions rather than as slogans.
caveats: Axis choice is subjective; the map is a discussion and alignment tool, not a quantitative scoring model.
Brands from other industries are plot references for contrast, not direct competitors to benchmark against.

cards.title: Build Three Stylescapes Before Commissioning Custom Design
cards.summary: Use three wide-layout curated mood boards to preview a brand across touchpoints before investing in design work
cards.use_when: Choosing a visual direction for a store, packaging or campaign when the strategy is agreed but the look is not
steps: Identify the key themes from your discovery and definition work, then gather visual references that match each theme. Adjust the references so they sit together in harmony rather than reading as a random collection.

Arrange each direction on a wide layout that previews the brand across multiple touchpoints — packaging through digital screens — so the team sees application, not just a mood. This is the source's definition of a stylescape and its purpose: exploring directions quickly before paying for custom design.

Produce three distinct directions, each with a name and a clear personality. The Mode case study used 'Serious Fun' (clean, curated, colorful), 'Crafted Narrative' (editorial-inspired with rich contrasting colors), and 'Bits of Joy' (bright and fun, nostalgic lo-fi graphics). Name yours so feedback can be referenced by direction instead of by vague preference.

Present and evaluate against two tests: what resonates with the team, and how well each direction matches the previously defined brand values. Explicitly ask which elements people want borrowed across directions.

Combine winners into a final stylescape rather than treating the three as finalists to eliminate. In the case study, 'Crafted Narrative' was most popular for its dark green palette and typography, but bitmap typefaces from 'Bits of Joy' and illustrations from 'Serious Fun' were merged into a final direction named 'The Story of Craft', which then became the foundation for the full visual identity.
caveats: Stylescapes are exploration artifacts, not production design; expect and plan for the merge step.
Presenter opinion: the source treats three directions as the working number, not a measured optimum.

cards.title: Assign Typography by Job, Not by Taste
cards.summary: Mix serif, sans-serif, monospace and bitmap typefaces by the function each piece of copy performs
cards.use_when: Specifying a type system for a product page, packaging, or brand refresh where technical and emotional copy coexist
steps: Split your copy into jobs first — headers, body, technical or specification copy, and any historical or personality-driven moments — then pick typefaces that fit each job rather than choosing one family for everything.

In the Mode case study the allocation was: serif and sans-serif for header and body copy, a monospace font specifically for technical copy to highlight engineering, and selective bitmap-style typefaces as a nod to the history of computing and mechanical keyboards. Apply the same mapping to an ecommerce context: product spec tables and compatibility notes alongside expressive headline and body type.

Test combinations in a type specimen, then look at them in context on sample pages before committing. The source explicitly uses sample webpages for this, because a pairing that works in a specimen can fail against layout, image and button styles.
Keep specialty typefaces selective — the source describes bitmap as 'selective use' and a 'fun nod', not as a workhorse. Overuse dilutes the contrast that makes the specialty face meaningful.

Verify legibility and rendering across your actual surfaces (packaging print vs. screen) when choosing final pairings, since the source chose a palette and type system that had to work across physical and digital collateral.
caveats: The specific fonts chosen for Mode are case-study specifics, not a recommended stack for other brands.
Bitmap and highly stylized faces are risky for long copy and accessibility; the source only assigns them decorative and referential roles.

cards.title: Anchor a Brand Palette with One Core Color and Supporting Accents
cards.summary: Choose one memorable anchor color plus a manageable set of accent colors that work across print and screen
cards.use_when: Establishing or refreshing the color system for a store, packaging, and acquisition creative that must stay consistent everywhere
steps: Start from the brand themes rather than from trending colors. In the Mode case study the anchor was a deep green chosen because it felt bold yet calming through its tie to nature, which directly expressed the 'Warm Tech' positioning.
Select a small set of secondary colors explicitly designated as accents. The source's structure is one anchor color with supporting accent colors, not a flat palette of equals.

Review swatches and combinations in multiple dedicated sessions and check them across every surface you ship: physical packaging and on-screen website at minimum. The source calls this one of the most intense parts of the process because color affects so much of the brand and business.

Where the palette feels unresolved, allow the merge behavior seen with stylescapes: in the case study the dark green palette from one direction was the reason that direction was preferred, and it survived the merge into the final direction.

Specify usage in your brand guidelines once decided — which color carries backgrounds, which marks actions and highlights — so future merchandising and ad creative stays consistent without re-deciding.
caveats: The source gives no contrast or accessibility thresholds; test legibility yourself for text on every chosen color.
Screen and print reproduction differ; a swatch review on one medium is not sufficient validation.

cards.title: Set Photography Rules as Explicit Constraints
cards.summary: Define a short list of photographic constraints so product imagery stays cohesive across vendors and channels
cards.use_when: Briefing product photography or UGC for a store, packaging, or social creative where images currently look inconsistent
steps: Write down the principles rather than collecting loose references. The Mode principles were: strong directional lighting; warm and natural tones with subtle film grain; scenes that feel lived-in but not messy; and people featured in a way that does not detract from the product.

Pair each rule with reference images that best capture that quality, so the brief is both verbal and visual. The source explicitly pairs rules with references to give the internal team enough guidance to capture photos and videos in the new direction.

Apply the rules to the decision of whether people appear in a shot. The rule that people must not detract from the product implies a merchandising constraint — human presence is context, not the subject, so the product remains the focus of a PDP image.

Institutionalize the rules in your brand guidelines and set up a capture environment for them. Mode's team built a dedicated studio setup to shoot photos and video that roll out on the site and in content, which is how the rules actually get followed at volume.
Use the same constraints for third-party and user content selection: lived-in but not messy is a usable inclusion filter for curated UGC on product pages.
caveats: These four rules are this brand's chosen style, not a universal best practice; a clinical or high-tech brand might deliberately choose the opposite.
Film grain and warm grading can misrepresent product color; test against accuracy requirements before adopting.

cards.title: Strip Technical Jargon from Product and Marketing Copy
cards.summary: Write a brand voice that is human, confident and clear even in a technical product category
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, specs pages, emails or ads for a technically complex product where copy has drifted into insider language
steps: Set the target balance explicitly. The source's stated goal was professional but not corporate, friendly but not fake, and it describes this as a difficult balance to strike — write the two poles down as a copy review test.

Assume your buyer is not a specialist. Even though the keyboard world is full of technical jargon, the source makes a conscious effort to use clear, simple language anyone can understand, on the reasoning that newcomers and enthusiasts both need to buy.

Draft core messages collaboratively in a shared document and refine them over multiple passes. Mode used a Notion document to write and refine core messages so word choices felt authentic rather than imposed.

Ban marketing buzzwords and favor honest, straightforward communication. Keep the emotional promise concrete — the source's themes were 'making technology feel more human and inviting' and 'creating joy in everyday experiences', expressed plainly rather than as abstract brandspeak.

Produce messaging samples attached to specific placements (website, marketing) rather than a general tone document, and keep a separate set of thought-starter 'brand expressions' showing the voice applied across physical and digital surfaces for future launches and events.
caveats: Voice work was done by an internal team with an outside facilitator; a solo operator should expect more drafting rounds to reach the same clarity.
Simplifying does not mean removing necessary specs — the source keeps deep technical information available for research-heavy buyers and reserves simple language for messaging.

cards.title: Segment Buyers by Behavior, Not Just Demographics
cards.summary: Build contrasting personas whose buying behavior demands different marketing and site treatments
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure a product page, catalog, or campaign when the audience ranges from expert hobbyists to busy first-time buyers
steps: Gather qualitative input specifically about why people buy or pass. The source combined website traffic and sales data analysis, customer surveys in the community, and in-depth video interviews with specific community members.

Build personas with names, constraints, desires and stories, and make sure at least two of them require entirely different treatments. The Mode examples: Tim, an experienced UX design manager in Austin who researches extensively, values quality and community, knows the people behind brands, and would enjoy building keyboard kits; versus Jay, a young software engineer in San Francisco seeking a workspace upgrade, who is busy, relies on influencer and publication recommendations, and wants a simple purchase process and ready-to-use products.

Derive concrete site requirements from each persona's behavior rather than stopping at description. For the researcher persona the conclusion is detailed product information plus visible community; for the busy persona it is a simple purchase path with clear guidance and pre-built options.

Concentrate exercise time on customers you do not already understand. Mode knew many current customers by name, so the segmentation work focused on attracting new ones — apply the same rule when your repeat base is already well understood.
Map each persona's journey from discovery to purchase and record what influences their decision and what holds them back, so the hurdles become a to-do list for pages, creative and messaging.
caveats: The Tim and Jay personas are illustrative constructs from one company's research, not validated segments you can copy.
Video interviews and community surveys give qualitative direction; they do not by themselves size a segment.

cards.title: Sequence a Site Redesign: Sitemap, Two Sample Pages, Then Rollout
cards.summary: Validate components and typography on two placeholder pages before building the full site
cards.use_when: Planning a store redesign or major template overhaul that must serve both newcomer and expert journeys
steps: Create a comprehensive sitemap first — a bird's-eye view of every page and route. The source describes this as challenging to think through but valuable because it forces you to plan all the paths a user can take and test different journeys so customers find what they need.

Then build two key pages using placeholder content. This reveals the overall aesthetic and the components you actually need — menus, typography styles, buttons, galleries — before production work begins.
Test typography and brand elements in context on those two pages before rolling the design out to the rest of the site, since some pairings only fail against real layout.

Design the routing to serve both a simple path and a deep-information path. The Mode goal was an experience that feels intuitive whether you are a first-time visitor or an enthusiast, with purchasing simplified for the busy persona and expanded brand and community content for the curious one.

Expect the remaining pages to take weeks of creation and refinement after the two samples are approved. Roll out gradually rather than as a single launch. The source's site was rolled out slowly through the year as development proceeded.
Revisit earlier work as you learn. The source notes that four months in, the team iterated on its earliest assets to keep everything cohesive and pointed at the stated goals.
caveats: The two-sample-page step is this team's approach, not a measured conversion finding; two pages may not expose every component your store needs.
Placeholder-page approval reduces rework but does not eliminate it — the source still iterated on early work during delivery.

cards.title: Define Brand Attributes Through Clustered Team Brainstorming
cards.summary: Turn free-form internal brainstorming into a prioritized, evidence-linked set of brand attributes
cards.use_when: Establishing the internal foundation for a store's positioning, voice, and look before any design or copy work begins
steps: Examine the brand through four separate lenses in sequence: values and beliefs, features and benefits, voice and tone, and look and feel. The source runs these as separate exercises rather than one combined discussion.

Use focused prompts to brainstorm freely within each lens, then group similar ideas and prioritize what resonates most deeply. The resulting word clusters become the themes that shape the brand's characteristics — described as attributes the company already embodies plus ideals to keep pursuing.
Do this before competitive mapping, because the attributes are the raw material for choosing the axes. In the source the positioning exercise follows directly from the attribute work.

Include the operators who own the outcome, not only creatives. Mode's session included the CEO, head of marketing, the design lead, and an outside facilitator who provided an objective perspective and served as a sounding board.

Use an external facilitator deliberately if you can: the source brought in an old collaborator specifically so the design lead could focus on crafting the vision while someone else guided the process and challenged ideas.
caveats: Facilitator sourcing is a service-vendor decision; a solo operator can substitute a structured written exercise, but should expect less challenge to assumptions.
Attribute lists are only useful if they later constrain real decisions — the source carries them into positioning, type, color and voice.

cards.title: Turn Vision into Three Written Design Challenges
cards.summary: Convert discovery insights into explicit design challenges that scope the rest of the work
cards.use_when: Moving from research to execution on a store rebrand, and needing a filter for what gets built and what gets cut
steps: Synthesize the discovery phase into patterns and themes that the whole team recognizes rather than a report nobody uses. Mode's emerging themes were 'Warm Tech' (making technology feel human and inviting), 'creating joy in everyday experiences' (keyboards should delight, not just function), and 'making products that deserve to exist' (quality and innovation rather than adding noise).

Accept that a vision alone is insufficient — the source pairs it with hard decisions about the product lineup, including discontinuing certain products to sharpen focus on better ones. Decide what you will stop selling.

Write the challenges as 'How might we…' questions that cover both physical product and digital experience. Mode's three: how might we create products that feel thoughtfully crafted rather than mass-produced, objects that bring joy and warmth to people's spaces; how might we design a brand identity that feels high-end and curated while still humble and human; how might we design a website that guides both newcomers and experienced enthusiasts through their journey.

Carry the challenges into every subsequent phase as the acceptance test for stylescapes, typography, color, site structure and product design — the source treats 'Warm Tech' explicitly as the north star of product design.

Let customer language sharpen the challenge. A customer comment that a nice keyboard can be like a piece of furniture that ties the room together became a guiding product principle: elevate the workspace and bring delight, the way good furniture transforms a room.
caveats: The three challenges are specific to Mode's situation; write your own from your discovery output rather than adopting theirs.
The source does not quantify how much revenue discontinued products represented; treat assortment cuts as a strategic judgment requiring its own data review.

cards.title: Document Logo Usage, Language Rules and Brand Expressions in a Brand Book
cards.summary: Package the identity system into a usable guideline set, including a separate expressive alter-ego layer
cards.use_when: Publishing brand guidelines after a redesign so that merchandising, packaging and campaign creative stay consistent
steps: Start the guidelines with logo usage rules. In the Mode case the existing logo was kept because it worked and carried built-in brand equity; the work went into slight refinements and detailed usage rather than a replacement.
Document the chosen typography, colors and imagery rules in one cohesive visual language so anyone producing packaging, site or ad assets has a single reference.
Write explicit language rules plus ready messaging samples for website and marketing use, so voice is applied rather than described.

Create a separate brand expressions guide showing the brand applied across physical and digital platforms. The source is explicit that these are not final products but thought-starters to draw from when creating future launch and event assets.

Formalize a secondary visual language where one has emerged. Mode developed lo-fi bitmap imagery inspired by retro computing as the 'alter-ego' of the brand, driving custom iconography, a logo variant, and a photo treatment. Keeping it as a named, contained layer lets it add personality without contaminating the core system.
caveats: These outputs formed at roughly four months and rollout continued for months after; the guidelines were incomplete and still being extended rather than a finished artifact.
The source stresses that the last 10% of refinement takes the most time and effort after reaching roughly 90% completion, so budget disproportionately for finalization.

cards.title: Measure Brand Progress Through Delivery Artifacts, Not Just Strategy
cards.summary: Track the concrete outputs a rebrand should produce so the work reaches the market instead of staying on slides
cards.use_when: Planning the delivery side of a store rebrand and deciding what has to ship for the project to count as done
steps: Convert the identity into shippable artifacts with named owners: finalized brand identity guidelines, a website redesign, updated packaging, a content capture setup, and a next-generation product. In Mode's delivery phase these were the concrete outputs.

Include operational changes, not only visuals. The source moved from foam inserts to recyclable molded pulp packaging starting with the next product run, paired with the new brand look — a materials change that carries the brand promise into the unboxing experience.

Build or commission the content capability to sustain the new imagery rules. Mode's team set up a studio to capture photos and video that roll out on the site and in future content, so the photography principles can be followed continuously.
Plan for a slow, phased launch. The source describes the delivery phase taking months to roll out fully with ongoing work after that, and notes that impact takes time to see.
Set an explicit expectation inside the team that reaching roughly 90% completion is relatively straightforward while the final 10% takes the most time, so schedules include a heavy refinement tail.
caveats: The Mode result set (guidelines, site, packaging, studio, next product) is one company's output list; your store may need a different or smaller set.
No outcome metrics are given in the source, so these artifacts should not be read as evidence of revenue impact.

cards.title: Use Customer Research to Choose Marketing Channels
cards.summary: Let the discovered moment of brand connection dictate where to invest marketing effort
cards.use_when: Allocating marketing budget between events, community, content and paid channels for a physical product
steps: Look for the specific moment customers say they connect with your brand. In Mode's research the most valuable insight was that people connect when they experience the keyboards firsthand, and the 'aha moment' occurs when they see and type on the products.

Convert that insight into a channel decision rather than a general 'be customer-centric' statement. Based on this finding the source plans to attend more in-person creative and tech events to create meaningful connections and grow the community, rather than defaulting to digital reach alone.

Pair channel choice with a transparency strategy. Mode's marketing emphasis became sharing more of the story, behind-the-scenes content, and introducing the team behind the brand — content formats that suit a brand built on human craft.

For stores selling a tactile product without in-person events, translate the finding into the closest digital equivalent: hands-on unboxing content, community showcases, and returns policies that lower the risk of buying without touching the product. The source's demonstrated result is event attendance; the ecommerce adaptation is an inference, not a tested outcome.

Re-check the channel decision against the personas. A discovery-led channel serves the researcher persona well, but the busy persona who relies on influencer and publication recommendations will still need a separate channel plan.
caveats: The source's finding is qualitative and brand-specific; a product whose value is fully conveyed by images or specs may not show the same hands-on trigger.
No measured attribution or lift is provided for the event strategy.

04-BRD / brand Goes here. The end-to-end framework for rebranding a physical product company using the Double Diamond process (Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver). Includes competitive positioning via XY mapping, defining brand attributes and voice, selecting typography and color palettes, and creating "Stylescapes" (mood boards) to translate abstract concepts into concrete visual identities. Not here. • Conducting the initial customer research and avatar interviews -> 02-AVT • Wireframing the website and mapping digital user journeys -> 07-LPG • Backend e-commerce store configuration and funding -> 05-SET

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the "Stylescape" methodology and specific visual rule-setting (e.g., photography lighting constraints, typography mixing) required to translate a strategic brand promise into a cohesive visual identity. modules: [BRD] topics: [brand positioning, visual identity, brand voice, stylescapes, competitive mapping] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. positioning / XY competitive mapping (e.g., warm/inviting vs. stark/industrial, transparent vs. opaque), formulating core brand themes (e.g., "Warm Tech", "creating joy in everyday experiences"); visual identity / Stylescapes (curated mood boards bridging abstract themes with visual execution), color palette selection (anchoring with a deep green and supporting accents), typography architecture (mixing serif, sans-serif, monospace for technical copy, and bitmap for retro nods); photography / establishing strict visual principles (strong directional lighting, warm tones, film grain, lived-in scenes); verbal identity / eliminating technical jargon, establishing a human and confident tone; brand book schema / brand expressions, logo usage, defining an "alter-ego" visual language.

Look for.

The Stylescape Method: Creating three distinct, wide-layout mood boards (e.g., "Serious Fun," "Crafted Narrative," "Bits of Joy") to preview how the brand looks across all physical and digital touchpoints before investing in custom design.

XY Positioning Mapping: Plotting competitors and out-of-industry brands on a grid with opposing qualities to identify crowded pools and carve out a unique visual/tonal space.

Photography Rules: Explicit constraints for brand imagery: strong directional lighting, warm/natural tones, subtle film grain, and scenes that feel "lived-in but not messy."

Typography Mixing: Assigning specific fonts to brand jobs (e.g., monospace for engineering/technical copy, bitmap for historical/retro nods).

Skip. Mentions of Shopify Capital, business funding mechanics, or generic statements about keyboards.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (the foundational process of establishing visual and verbal identity). Volume. ~400 words.

02-AVT / avatars and jobs to be done Goes here. Customer discovery methodology, mapping the buyer journey, and constructing distinct user personas based on varying levels of market sophistication and buying behaviors. Not here. • Designing the visual brand elements to appeal to these avatars -> 04-BRD • Structuring the website navigation to guide the personas -> 07-LPG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Demonstrates how to translate qualitative video interviews and community surveys into actionable user personas with opposing buying behaviors and informational needs. modules: [AVT] topics: [customer research, user personas, customer journey mapping, interview techniques] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. research method / conducting community surveys, executing in-depth video interviews to uncover buying vs. passing motivations, analyzing historical sales and traffic data; segmentation / creating distinct user personas with specific constraints, desires, and stories; jobs and trigger moments / mapping the interaction from discovery to purchase, identifying friction points and hurdles.

Look for.

Contrasting Avatar Structures: Creating personas that require entirely different marketing treatments. For example, "Tim" (an experienced UX manager who researches extensively, values community, and requires deep technical specs) versus "Jay" (a busy software engineer who relies on influencer recommendations, wants a simple purchase process, and needs ready-to-use products).

Journey Mapping: Documenting exactly what influences each specific persona's decisions and what specific hurdles hold them back from purchasing.

Skip. General business growth goals or product manufacturing details.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (understanding the customer before positioning the brand). Volume. ~250 words.

07-LPG / landing pages Goes here. Structuring a website to cater to multiple persona journeys, developing sitemaps, and testing wireframes/placeholder content before full development. Not here. • Defining the visual identity and colors applied to the site -> 04-BRD • Installing the Shopify backend, payments, and tracking -> 05-SET

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Outlines the exact sequence for overhauling a brand website, emphasizing sitemap creation and placeholder-content testing to validate multiple user journeys before full design and development. modules: [LPG] topics: [sitemaps, user journeys, wireframing, page structuring] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. page types and section order / sitemap creation, bird's-eye view of all pages and routing; friction removal / testing user journeys to ensure easy navigation for both beginners (simple purchase paths) and enthusiasts (deep informational paths); wireframing / using placeholder content on key pages to test aesthetics and component layout.

Look for.

The Digital Design Sequence: 1. Create a comprehensive sitemap to map all possible user paths. 2. Build two key pages using placeholder content to test components (menus, galleries, buttons) and evaluate the overall aesthetic. 3. Test typography and brand elements in context on these sample pages before rolling out the design to the rest of the site.

Skip. Shopify ad reads, flexible funding options, and backend e-commerce operations.

Scope mix. 100% baseline. Volume. ~200 words.

At the start of 2025, I joined Mode as their Chief Design Officer. My first task? Reimagining the company's brand. But where do you begin? How do you position your brand to stand out from competitors? Why risk changing something that already works? And how can a rebrand transform a business and shape its future products? Hello, I'm Matthew Encina. In this video, I’ll walk you through the process of building a brand, from start to finish. Thanks to Shopify for sponsoring this video. Before we begin, I’ll give a little context on how we got here. The story of Mode begins when our founder Jaicob discovers mechanical keyboards while working as a software engineer. What starts as a hobby—building his first custom keyboard—evolves into a quest for the perfect typing experience. This obsession sparks ideas that lead to late-night designing, which becomes Mode's first product: a batch of 50 keyboards. No outside investments. No crowdfunding. No guarantee of success. The keyboard isn't perfect—first attempts rarely are—but 50 incredible humans take a chance on Mode. Since then, Mode has grown steadily, reinvesting in better keyboards with each production run. Now, five years later, it has transformed from a side project into a company with a clear vision: Mode isn't just about keyboards—it's about how thoughtful design transforms everyday experiences. This vision comes to life through our small, dedicated remote team across Boston, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. That’s where I come in. As a creative professional in design, advertising, and branding since 2003, I've collaborated with some of the biggest brands in the world. My path takes an unexpected turn when my own keyboard obsession leads me to explore industrial product design. In 2022, I discover Mode and instantly connect with their design aesthetic. As a DIY project, I create an oak accent piece for their Sonnet keyboard—I love how wood brings warmth to tech peripherals. This becomes an official Mode product and leads to a bigger project: designing an entire keyboard from scratch. These successes, combined with my experience, pave the way for me to join Mode as Chief Design Officer in 2025, where I now lead the brand and product vision. It's a huge responsibility, but I'm thrilled by what’s next. You might be wondering: if a company is doing well, why change anything? Over the last five years, we’ve grown and developed clearer opinions on what we want Mode to be, what values drive our product design, and how we want to do business. So we want to update the brand to reflect that. The questions on our minds are: Where have we been in the last five years, and what’s our vision for Mode in the future? How might we position our brand and products to be distinct in the marketplace? What‘s worth keeping and what needs to change for our business to grow? And this is where the branding process comes in. While most people associate a brand with its logo, colors, and typefaces, it's so much more than that. "A brand is a person's gut feeling about a product, service, or company." Every touchpoint and interaction shapes how customers perceive the brand. A strong brand: Has an outstanding reputation Is perceived as valuable Stands out from competitors Forms genuine connections with customers Our branding process examines all aspects of our business—positioning, product, culture, and customers—to determine what changes will help us achieve our goals. This process takes several weeks and follows the Double Diamond framework. A brand refresh is no easy task, and while I'm up for the challenge, it's always good to have an extra creative mind to collaborate with. This is Ben Burns, an old co-worker and friend. He's a well-rounded creative with excellent taste. As the former Digital Director at Blind and Chief Operating Officer at The Futur, we collaborated on numerous client projects and digital products together. When Ben became available for design work, I jumped at the chance to bring him on board to facilitate our branding process. With Ben's involvement, I can focus on crafting the brand vision while he provides an objective outside perspective, serving as both a sounding board for ideas and a skilled hand in bringing them to life. First, we begin with the Discover Phase. We expand our understanding of the brand vision, business goals, and challenges while gathering data on products, customers, and the market. We kick off our Discovery process by getting the team together at my LA studio. The crew includes Jaicob (our CEO), Xris (our Head of Marketing), myself, and Ben, who guides us through the session. Before jumping into the brand exercises, we took some time to align on our bigger company goals. Here's what rose to the top: Establish a distinct brand voice with a clear identity and point of view. deepen our understanding of current customers while identifying and planning for new ones. Update and refine our product catalog to better serve our customers and reflect our brand. And, increase revenue over the next 5 years to invest in more challenging projects. Before our meetup, we spend weeks gathering research and data. We analyze website traffic, sales data, and conduct customer surveys within the keyboard community to understand trends and preferences. We also do in-depth video interviews with specific community members to learn why they buy or pass on our products. These insights inform our in-person user exercises, where we identify and segment our current and future customer base to better understand who we serve. We know our current customers–many by name– so we focus our exercises on how we can attract new ones. Our research helps us create detailed user personas with names and stories that reveal what matters to these potential customers. We then map how each customer type interacts with our brand from discovery to purchase, noting what influences their decisions and what holds them back. This helps us spot hurdles we need to address. There were many customers we considered, but here are two examples of personas and their journeys: First is Tim, an experienced UX Design Manager in Austin, Texas. He extensively researches products before purchasing. Tim values quality, community, and knowing the people behind the brands. As a hobby enthusiast, he’d likely enjoy building our keyboard kits. For customers like Tim, we need detailed product information available and to make the community around our brand visible. Then there's Jay, a young software engineer in San Francisco, California who's seeking a workspace upgrade. Jay is busy, so he doesn’t want to spend a lot of time trying to find a better keyboard. He relies on influencer and publication recommendations. For him, we need a simple purchase process with clear guidance and the option for ready-to-use products. Looking at different user types gives us a valuable perspective on improving our products and customer experience. With these insights, we now turn our focus inward to examine our brand. In the next series of exercises, we examine our brand through multiple lenses: values and beliefs, features and benefits, voice and tone, and look and feel. Using focused prompts, our team brainstorms freely. We group similar ideas and prioritize what resonates most deeply. The word clusters reveal clear themes that shape our brand's characteristics. These are attributes we currently embody and ideals we will continue to pursue as we grow the brand. Using the brand attributes defined from our prompts, we analyze our positioning in the competitive landscape. Positioning is the space a brand occupies in the hearts and minds of customers, relative to competitors. For our exercise, we create an X&Y map with opposing brand qualities. We plot both our competitors and brands from other industries to visualize where we stand in the market. For our voice, we ask: Are we understated or outspoken? Are we an opaque company or more transparent and human? For our aesthetic: Are we warm and inviting or stark and industrial? Are we highly curated or raw and unedited? Are our products expensive, or are they budget options? Are they considered premium or the standard? What we find is eye-opening and sparks a lot of discussion. In some areas, we are swimming in a crowded pool without much to set us apart. This realization pushes us to ask important questions: How can we carve out our own unique space? What do we need to change to create distinction from our competitors? This helps us refine our brand positioning as we wrap up our work for the Discovery Phase. Moving into the Define phase, we synthesize everything we learned during Discovery to clarify our design challenge. The research and discussions helped us understand our business better and where we fit in the market. These insights come together during our LA meeting, but become even clearer as we reflect on them over the following weeks. What emerges is a clear vision for Mode's future. We start seeing patterns and themes that resonate with everyone on the team. Ideas like "Warm Tech" - making technology feel more human and inviting. "Creating joy in everyday experiences" - because keyboards shouldn't just be functional, they should bring delight. And "making products that deserve to exist" - focusing on quality and innovation rather than just adding to the noise. But having a vision isn't enough. We have to make some tough decisions about our product lineup. This means taking a hard look at our current offerings and being honest about what needs to change. As a result, we're discontinuing certain products to sharpen our focus on better ones. We also know our visual identity, messaging, and website need a complete overhaul to better serve our customers and reflect our new direction. In this Define Phase, we have a clear set of Design Challenges to address in the rest of the process: How might we create products that feel thoughtfully crafted rather than mass-produced—objects that bring joy and warmth to people's spaces? How might we design a brand identity that feels high-end and curated while still feeling humble and human? How might we design a website that seamlessly guides both newcomers and experienced enthusiasts through their journey? We want the shopping experience to be simple and smooth, so we use Shopify, the sponsor of this video. Shopify is a powerful set of tools that helps you start and manage your business, whether online or in-person. When Mode started its keyboard business in 2019, managing an e-commerce operation while developing its first product felt overwhelming. Thanks to Shopify, setting up a store was simple, letting Mode focus on delivering their first product. As Mode grew, maintaining enough capital to fund orders became crucial for operations. Shopify Capital provides flexible funding that you can repay as you sell, accessible at every stage of growth, right from your dashboard. This enables businesses like ours to seize opportunities by improving cash flow—especially when investing in inventory to maintain steady sales. Shopify is there for you when you’re just starting out, and grows with your business. It has apps to build and customize your store and ways to connect and sell natively on social platforms to meet your customers where they are. Thanks to Shopify for sponsoring this video. Go to shopify.com/matthewencina to learn more. Now that we have our direction, we move into expansive exploration in the Develop Phase, exploring ideas for the new brand and creating solutions that address our goals. We begin with stylescapes, which are carefully curated mood boards. This is a process Ben and I use to transform abstract ideas into concrete visuals, allowing us to explore different design directions quickly before we invest time in custom design work. Drawing from our Discovery and Define phases, we identify key themes that shape each direction. We gather visual references that match these themes, adjust them to create visual harmony, and arrange them on a wide layout. Stylescapes provide a preview of how the brand looks across different touchpoints, from packaging to digital screens. We develop three distinct directions to present to the Mode team: First, there’s "Serious Fun" - clean, curated, and colorful Next, "Crafted Narrative" - inspired by editorial design with rich, contrasting colors Lastly, "Bits of Joy" - bright and fun, with a modern take at nostalgic lo-fi graphics During the presentation, we look for what resonates with the team and how well each direction matches our defined brand values. The second direction proves to be most popular, particularly for its dark green palette and typography choices. The team also likes elements from the other directions, including the bitmap typefaces from "Bits of Joy" and illustrations from "Serious Fun." Based on this feedback, we combine the best elements to create our final stylescape, "The Story of Craft." This direction features editorial-inspired typography, hand-drawn elements, and maker marks that showcase our craftsmanship. Rich colors, warm tones, and imagery highlight how our products bring joy to spaces. This stylescape serves as our foundation for developing the complete visual identity. The first design project we take on is the website. It’s the largest asset we need to create, but also has the most opportunities to figure out many aspects of the brand, like typography, imagery, and colors. The goal is to create an experience that reflects our new brand and feels intuitive, whether you're a first-time visitor or a keyboard enthusiast. First, we create a sitemap, a bird's eye view of every page on the website. It's challenging to think through, but it allows us to plan for all the various paths a user can take on our site. This process allows us to test different user journeys, ensuring customers can easily find what they're looking for. Next, we create two key pages using placeholder content. This gives us a sense of the overall aesthetic and the components we need, like menus, typography styles, buttons, galleries, and more. Once we’re happy with these two pages, it takes us a few weeks to create and refine the rest of the website. Typography plays a big part of any brand identity. In our stylescapes, we determine that we want to use a combination of serif and sans-serif, for our header and body copy, and selective use of bitmap-style typefaces as a fun nod to the history of computing and mechanical keyboards. We can test different typeface combinations in a type specimen, and look at them in context on our sample webpages. We finally choose to add a monospace font for technical copy to highlight the engineering aspects of our work. Next is choosing our colors for the brand, which is more complex than you might think.
